readings.title: First reading
readings.text: One day as Elisha was on his way to Shunem, a woman of rank who lived there pressed him to stay and eat there. After this he always broke his journey for a meal when he passed that way. She said to her husband, ‘Look, I am sure the man who is constantly passing our way must be a holy man of God. Let us build him a small room on the roof, and put him a bed in it, and a table and chair and lamp; whenever he comes to us he can rest there.’ One day when he came, he retired to the upper room and lay down. He said to his servant Gehazi, ‘Call our Shunammitess. Tell her this: “Look, you have gone to all this trouble for us, what can we do for you? Is there anything you would like said for you to the king or to the commander of the army?”’ But she replied, ‘I live with my own people about me.’ ‘What can be done for her then?’ he asked. Gehazi answered, ‘Well, she has no son and her husband is old.’ Elisha said, ‘Call her.’ The servant called her and she stood at the door. This time next year,’ he said ‘you will hold a son in your arms.’

exegesis.summary: The wealthy Shunammite woman recognizes Elisha as a holy man of God and extends extraordinary hospitality, building him a room with bed, table, chair, and lamp. Her generosity, offered without expectation of reward, is met by a divine gift beyond her hoping: she who has no son will hold a child in her arms within the year. The passage reveals that welcoming God's prophet is welcoming God Himself, and such welcome bears fruit in the gift of life.

patristicQuotes.quote: A happy exchange! In place of gold and silver, they received power to heal the sick, to raise the dead. He made them angels more than men, freeing them from all anxiety of this life, that they might have but one care, that of teaching.
Behold the accomplishment of this saying; to whatsoever part of the world you go, you will find this woman famous, and this has been wrought by the power of Him who spake this word.

cccReferences.title: The prophetic ministry of Elijah and Elisha
Our hearts restless until they rest in God

exegesis.thematicConnection: This reading sets the template for Jesus' promise in the Gospel that 'anyone who welcomes a prophet will have a prophet's reward.' The Shunammite is the model disciple who recognizes the man of God and receives him; her reward of a son foreshadows the new life given to those who welcome Christ's messengers.

readings.title: Responsorial Psalm
readings.text:
I will sing for ever of your love, O Lord.
I will sing for ever of your love, O Lord;
through all ages my mouth will proclaim your truth.
Of this I am sure, that your love lasts for ever,
that your truth is firmly established as the heavens.
I will sing for ever of your love, O Lord.
Happy the people who acclaim such a king,
who walk, O Lord, in the light of your face,
who find their joy every day in your name,
who make your justice the source of their bliss.
I will sing for ever of your love, O Lord.
For it is you, O Lord, who are the glory of their strength;
by your favour it is that our might is exalted;
for our ruler is in the keeping of the Lord;
our king in the keeping of the Holy One of Israel.
I will sing for ever of your love, O Lord.
readings.refrain: I will sing for ever of your love, O Lord.

exegesis.summary: The psalmist vows to sing forever of the Lord's enduring love and faithfulness, which is as steadfast as the heavens themselves. He proclaims the blessedness of the people who walk in the light of God's face and find their joy in His name. The covenant love of God is the unshakable ground on which the believer's whole life is built.

patristicQuotes.quote: To the prophet who asks, 'What man is he that liveth, and shall not see death?' (Ps. 88) we are able to answer, He who keepeth Christ's word.
This promise of heritage shall not be narrowed by any limits, but to the very end of time there shall never lack believers, the glory of whose happiness shall be everlasting.

cccReferences.title: Love as the source of prayer

exegesis.thematicConnection: The psalm's song of God's faithful love undergirds every other reading: it is this hesed that raises the Shunammite's barrenness to life, that raises us with Christ from the waters of Baptism, and that makes the smallest cup of cold water given for Christ's sake an eternal treasure.

readings.title: Second reading
readings.text: When we were baptised in Christ Jesus we were baptised in his death; in other words, when we were baptised we went into the tomb with him and joined him in death, so that as Christ was raised from the dead by the Father’s glory, we too might live a new life.

exegesis.summary: St. Paul proclaims that Baptism is no mere ritual but a real participation in the death and resurrection of Christ. Plunged into His tomb through the sacrament, we rise to walk in newness of life, dead to sin and alive to God in Christ Jesus. This is the radical reconfiguration of our existence that makes possible the total self-gift Jesus demands in the Gospel.

patristicQuotes.quote: Christ comes also to baptism perhaps to sanctify baptism, but doubtless to bury the old Adam in water.

We are baptized by the Lord in the Holy Ghost, not only when in the day of our baptism we are washed in the fount of life, but also daily by the grace of the same Spirit we are inflamed to do those things which please God.

cccReferences.title: Baptism as descent into the tomb with Christ
Buried with Christ, raised with Him
Sacramental assimilation to Christ's death and resurrection

exegesis.thematicConnection: Paul provides the theological key for the Gospel's hard sayings. To lose one's life for Christ's sake and find it is precisely what was sacramentally accomplished in Baptism: we have already died with Him, so taking up the cross is simply living out the identity we received in the font.

readings.title: Gospel
readings.text: Jesus instructed the Twelve as follows: ‘Anyone who prefers father or mother to me is not worthy of me. Anyone who prefers son or daughter to me is not worthy of me. Anyone who does not take his cross and follow in my footsteps is not worthy of me. Anyone who finds his life will lose it; anyone who loses his life for my sake will find it.

exegesis.summary: Jesus concludes His missionary discourse with words of stark demand and tender promise. Discipleship requires loving Him above every natural bond, taking up the cross, and losing one's life to find it. Then He turns to those who receive His apostles: whoever welcomes them welcomes Him, and even a cup of cold water given to one of His little ones will not lose its reward.

patristicQuotes.quote: Nothing is nearer to a man than his soul, and yet He enjoins that this should not only be hated, but that a man should be ready to deliver it up to death... He had as yet said nothing to them respecting his own sufferings, but instructs them in the meanwhile in these things, that they may the more readily receive His words concerning His passion.

cccReferences.title: Conformed to the image of His Son
Christ's love excludes no one, even 'little ones'

exegesis.thematicConnection: The Gospel gathers up the day's readings: the welcome of the Shunammite becomes the welcome of any disciple who receives Christ's messengers; the baptismal death-to-self of Romans becomes the daily cross; and the Lord's everlasting love sung in the psalm is the reward awaiting even the smallest act of love done in His name.

synthesis.title: The Cost of Welcome, the Gift of New Life
synthesis.body: Today the Church places before us the strange arithmetic of the Kingdom: what we give away, we gain; what we cling to, we lose; and the smallest gesture of welcome offered to Christ's own bears a reward beyond all calculation. The Shunammite woman opens her home to Elisha without asking anything in return, and God opens her womb to life. Centuries later, Jesus tells His apostles that whoever receives them receives Him, and whoever receives Him receives the Father who sent Him — and even a cup of cold water given to one of His little ones is remembered forever. Between these two scenes stands the cross. Christ does not ask us to love Him more than father, mother, son, or daughter as if competing for affection, but because He alone is the source from whom all true love flows. The psalm sings the reason: the Lord's love endures forever, and those who walk in the light of His face find joy in His name. St. Paul tells us how this becomes possible: in Baptism we have already died with Christ and risen to new life. The cross we take up today is simply the unfolding of what was sacramentally given at the font. To lose our life for His sake is to discover it, finally and forever, hidden with Christ in God.
